top_categories.workout_context: 390 miles. Your legs will beg to quit after 120. This trains the power output you need from mile 130 onward.
27,000ft of climbing makes aerobic ceiling relevant when the grade or pace changes. VO2max work supports those hard moments; sustained climbing and conservative pacing remain the spine.
Every hard session works better with a bigger aerobic base. At 390 miles, base fitness is the difference between racing and surviving.
Race-pace efforts that mimic Ride the Rockies' demands. Pacing, fueling, and tactical decisions under fatigue. Practice the race before June.
At Ride the Rockies, changes in grade or pace can lift effort above threshold before it settles again. Over-unders train that transition while you keep riding.
27,000ft of climbing on grades that change every minute. You need to switch from seated to standing without losing rhythm.
69ft/mi signals a climbing-heavy course. Sustained sub-threshold and threshold work builds the steady power needed without turning the opening climb into the day’s hardest effort.

Road-specific control matters at Ride the Rockies. Practice on paved mountain highways and county roads: use smooth gear and cadence changes, accelerate deliberately out of corners, and settle quickly back into sustainable power for 390 miles.
390 miles rewards fat oxidation. This volume work shifts your fuel mix so you're still burning fat at hour 5, not bonking at hour 3.
Endurance with intensity spikes baked in. Exactly what 27,000ft of climbing on paved mountain highways and county roads does to your power file on race day.
88–92% FTP is where you'll spend the hardest sustained miles of Ride the Rockies. Train it until it feels boring.
Low-cadence force work supports 27,000ft of climbing when the grade lowers cadence. Practice controlled torque while preserving good form.

race_overlay.weather: June in Colorado Rocky Mountains (route changed annually) — Mid-June in the Colorado Rockies brings warm valley temps (75-90F) with significantly cooler conditions at pass summits (40-55F). Afternoon thunderstorms are near-daily above treeline. Lightning exposure on open passes is a genuine safety concern. UV intensity at altitude is severe. Rehearse adaptable layers and race-day kit changes in the final 2 weeks, including rain protection and wet-road braking before Ride the Rockies. Use the organizer's current forecast and safety instructions for final choices.
race_overlay.nutrition: Ultra-distance fueling for 390 miles: 80–100g carbs/hour from mile 1 — don’t wait until you’re hungry. Practice your exact race-day nutrition in every long training ride. Carry backup calories. 390 miles burns 8,000–12,000+ calories — you cannot replace them all, but you must try.
race_overlay.altitude: Ride the Rockies includes meaningful altitude exposure. Reduced oxygen availability can affect sustainable power, pacing, and recovery. Use a conservative upper-mountain pacing plan, test any travel or acclimatization strategy before the event, and plan layers for changing conditions. Do not begin iron or other supplements without clinician-guided testing. Afternoon thunderstorms above treeline — lightning is a real hazard at 10,000+ feet; Intense UV radiation at altitude — sunburn happens fast above 9,000 feet.

pack_summary: This 10-workout pack focuses on Durability, VO2max, and Endurance to prepare you for 390 miles of paved mountain highways and county roads in Colorado Rocky Mountains (route changed annually).
